summary: Many applications need two-way communication, so round-trip packet loss is often measured in practice. This RFC specifies a round-trip packet loss metric, following the framework of the IP performance metrics work and building on the capability of TWAMP in RFC 5357.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of checking if a ball arrives, you check if the ball makes it there and back. This defines the way to count lost round trips.

questions: how to measure round-trip packet loss
what is the round-trip loss metric
what is the round-trip loss ratio
subtitle: A precise definition of when a packet counts as lost on a there-and-back trip across an IP network.

tldr.problem: Two-way connectivity is what most applications need and round-trip loss is widely measured, yet no round-trip packet loss metric existed in the IP performance metrics framework of RFC 2330.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a singleton metric (one packet is either lost or not), a sample metric (a stream of such singletons) and a ratio statistic, adapting the one-way loss and round-trip delay metrics.
tldr.outcome: Round-trip loss is now a standard IPPM metric, with guidance on responder timing, reordering and the limits of inferring one-way loss.

today: RFC 6673 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the IPPM metrics with round-trip loss.

sections.title: Why Measure Round-Trip Loss
sections.content:
Failure to transfer a packet in either direction is a round-trip packet loss. The RFC points out that the TCP three-way handshake cannot complete without two-way connectivity in a near-simultaneous time interval, so round-trip loss gives a basis for inferring application performance.

Round-trip measurement also keeps test systems simple, because one host just echoes test packets back. Tools such as ping can measure it but usually need ICMP Echo support, and ICMP may be treated exceptionally on the path. The Two-Way Active Measurement Protocol (TWAMP, RFC 5357) already gives a round-trip loss capability, but there was no metric defined under the framework of RFC 2330.

A further reason: delay statistics are often reported only for packets that arrive, so lost packets need to be reported separately under a standardized metric.
sections.plainLanguage: Most things you do online need messages to go there and come back. So it helps to count how often the trip fails.

sections.title: Scope and Common Parameters
sections.content:
The memo defines a singleton metric, a sample metric and a statistic, following RFC 2330. That framework is for active measurement. The metric MAY also apply to passive measurement, but that is outside the normative scope. The memo also lists key considerations for inferring one-way loss from a two-way measurement.

The shared parameters include Src and Dst (host addresses), T and Tf (start and end of the test interval), lambda (rate for Poisson streams), incT and T0 (spacing and random start for periodic streams), TstampSrc (wire time at which a packet leaves Src), Tmax (the longest time Src waits for the reflected packet) and Type-P (any packet field that may affect treatment in the network). Per-packet results are logical values: 0 for success and 1 for loss.
sections.plainLanguage: Before counting, you agree on the rules: who throws, who catches, how long to wait, and what kind of ball to use.

sections.title: The Singleton Round-Trip Loss Metric
sections.content:
Type-P-Round-trip-Loss is 0 when Src sent a packet to Dst, Dst received it and sent a packet back as quickly as possible, and Src received the last bit of the reflected packet before TstampSrc + Tmax. It is 1 when Src did not receive the reflected packet before that waiting time ran out.

A loss of 1 can have three causes: Dst did not receive the packet, Dst did not send a packet back, or Src did not receive the reflected packet. Following RFC 2681, the RFC asserts that round-trip loss is the same whichever host starts the test.

For the responder, the RFC adds guidance: a responder serving typical loss testing SHOULD respond in 1 second or less. One that cannot SHOULD log the fact, and analysis of responder timestamps that finds slow responses SHOULD cause operator notification and the operator SHOULD suspend tests to that responder, since it may be overloaded.
sections.plainLanguage: If your ball is back before the timer runs out, that is a zero. If not, it is a one. You do not know which way it got lost, only that the trip failed.

sections.title: Samples, Streams and the Loss Ratio
sections.content:
A sample fixes Src, Dst and Type-P and chooses a set of send times. Two ways are named: Poisson, a pseudo-random process of rate lambda, and Periodic, with a pseudo-random start time T0 and nominal interval incT. The metric name replaces <Sample> with the process used. Another sample process may be used if it meets RFC 2330 and its details are reported.

Type-P-Round-trip-Loss-<Sample>-Stream is a sequence of pairs (TstampSrc, L). The statistic Type-P-Round-trip-Loss-<Sample>-Ratio is the average of all the L values in the stream, in units of lost packets per round-trip transmissions actually attempted. It is undefined if the sample is empty.

Packet reordering matters too. If packets arrive with sequence numbers 4, 7, 5, 6, then 5 and 6 are reordered but not lost. Methods should keep waiting the specified time and avoid declaring loss early, and implementations MUST address reordering.
sections.plainLanguage: Do the ball game many times, then work out what share of throws did not come back. If the ball just arrives out of order, it still counts as arrived.

sections.title: Round-Trip Testing and One-Way Reporting
sections.content:
Using a round-trip test to say something about each direction is tricky. Sampling of the reverse path depends on packets reaching Dst and on Dst replying, so appreciable loss on the forward path makes an assessment of the reverse path invalid. Reverse-path sample times also depend on forward delay and on Dst processing time, so appreciable delay variation on the forward path has the same effect.

Reordering on the forward path misaligns sequence numbers applied at Dst compared with the sender's, and implementations MUST address this.

On measurement setup, both hosts MUST be configured to send and receive the chosen Type-P. Every received test packet MUST produce a response, generated as quickly as possible, and these features MUST be calibrated under a representative load, with unexpected discards and errors recorded. The RFC notes that TWAMP can collect four timestamps, which helps identify path asymmetry or unexpected processing time at the responder.
sections.plainLanguage: If throws to your friend often fail, you cannot learn much about the way back. So be careful when you say which direction was bad.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The method sends a stream of packets to a destination and back, so it could be abused for denial-of-service attacks against the destination or the networks in between. The RFC advises bilateral or multilateral agreements on the timing, size and frequency of sample collection. Exceeding the agreed terms may be cause for rejecting packets.

Active use generates its own packets and does not threaten user data confidentiality. Passive measurement must restrict attention to headers of interest, and stored payloads MUST be kept safe and confidential.

Parties who can recognise sample packets might treat them differently or inject extra ones, distorting results. Authentication or encryption such as digital signatures MAY be used against injected traffic, and RFC 5357 includes both. No IANA action is requested, since the old IPPM metrics registry was declared obsolete in RFC 6248.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not flood someone with test throws without asking, and watch out for people who might cheat to make the numbers look better or worse.
